title: From Cabin Pressure to Gut Jet Lag: What Flying Really Does to Your Body
excerpt: New research reveals that long-haul flights disrupt not just sleep patterns but gut bacteria rhythms, while low cabin pressure, dehydration, and prolonged sitting create a cascade of physiological stress most travelers underestimate.
body:
• Cabin pressure at cruising altitude reduces blood oxygen saturation by 3–4%, equivalent to standing atop a 2,400-meter mountain, causing fatigue and shortness of breath even in healthy passengers.
  • New research from Wrocław Medical University shows long-haul flights disrupt gut bacteria rhythms — a phenomenon called "gut jet lag" — contributing to bloating, constipation, and low energy for days after arrival.
  • Prolonged immobility during flights raises venous thromboembolism risk up to four-fold, with 75% of air-travel blood clot cases linked to staying seated, according to a Lancet review.
  • Cabin humidity levels drop as low as 5–25%, well below the 30–60% range considered comfortable, drying out skin, nasal passages, and eyes.

The Thin Air at 35,000 Feet

When a commercial aircraft reaches cruising altitude, the cabin is pressurized to the equivalent of roughly 1,500 to 2,400 meters above sea level — not to the ground-level pressure most bodies are used to. The result, according to a comprehensive review published in The Lancet, is a drop in arterial oxygen partial pressure from about 95 mm Hg at sea level to around 60 mm Hg at maximum cabin altitude.

For healthy passengers, that translates to a 3–4% decrease in blood oxygen saturation. "Air pressure is lower at higher altitudes, which means your body takes in less oxygen," explains Dr. Matthew Goldman, a family medicine physician at Cleveland Clinic. "Airlines pressurize the air in the cabin, but not to sea-level pressures, so there's still less oxygen getting to your body when you fly."

The effects are subtle but real: fatigue, lightheadedness, headache. A study of adult volunteers simulating a 20-hour flight found that complaints associated with acute mountain sickness — fatigue, headache, lightheadedness, and nausea — increased with altitude and peaked at 2,438 meters, with most symptoms appearing after three to nine hours of exposure, according to the Lancet review.

Your Gut Has Its Own Jet Lag

Beyond the well-known circadian disruption of jet lag, researchers have now identified a parallel phenomenon playing out in the digestive system. A July 2026 study from Wrocław Medical University, published in the journal Nutrients, describes what the authors call "gut jet lag" — a desynchronization between the body's biological clock and the rhythms of trillions of gut bacteria.

"Our digestive system is extremely sensitive to these changes because the entire gut-brain axis operates according to a tightly regulated circadian rhythm. When biological signals become misaligned, communication between the intestines, immune system, and brain is temporarily disrupted."

— Kacper Wiśniewski, co-author, Wrocław Medical University

The disruption is not trivial. According to co-author Laura Rafner, a sudden shift in meal timing directly affects the secretion of digestive enzymes, bile production, and gastrointestinal motility. The gut microbiome may temporarily shift toward less beneficial bacterial strains, slowing intestinal transit and causing constipation, bloating, and discomfort.

The cabin environment compounds the problem. Gas in body cavities expands by roughly 30% at cruising altitude due to Boyle's law, according to the Lancet review. That expansion causes abdominal cramping and bloating — symptoms many flyers attribute to airplane food rather than physics.

Blood Clots, Dehydration, and the Risks of Sitting Still

Perhaps the most medically serious consequence of long flights is the elevated risk of venous thromboembolism — blood clots that typically form in the deep veins of the legs. The Lancet review calculated a pooled odds ratio of 1.59 from case-control studies, with risk climbing sharply when flights exceed eight hours. One population-based study of 9,000 business travelers found an absolute risk of one clot event every 4,656 flights.

Immobility is the primary driver. The Long-Flight Thrombosis Study (LONFLIT) found that 75% of air-travel blood clot cases involved passengers in non-aisle seats, where movement is most restricted. Dehydration worsens the picture by thickening blood and increasing its tendency to clot.

Cabin humidity plays a role here, too. About half the air circulating in a cabin is pulled from outside the aircraft at altitude, where it is nearly devoid of moisture, according to Cleveland Clinic. Interior humidity levels typically range from just 5% to 25% — far below the 30–60% range considered comfortable indoors. The result: dry skin, irritated eyes, and parched nasal passages, along with increased insensible fluid loss.

Practical Steps for Long-Haul Travelers

The research points to a handful of evidence-based countermeasures. Compression stockings with an ankle pressure of 17–30 mm Hg significantly reduce clot risk: a meta-analysis cited in the Lancet review found that only two of 1,237 passengers wearing compression stockings developed venous thrombosis, compared with 46 of 1,245 who did not.

For gut jet lag, the Wrocław researchers recommend gradually shifting sleep and meal schedules toward the destination time zone in the days before departure. "While on the plane and after landing, meals should be consumed only during the daytime hours of the destination time zone, while eating during your biological night should be strictly avoided," advises co-author Paweł Witko. Probiotic supplementation before travel may also help.

Hydration remains the simplest intervention across nearly every flight-related health concern. Dr. Goldman suggests packing an empty water bottle to refill after security rather than relying on the small servings from the beverage cart. Walking the cabin periodically and performing calf-muscle exercises in the seat can help maintain blood flow.

What's Next

The Wrocław study focused on athletes but its authors say the findings apply broadly — particularly to shift workers, airline personnel, and the millions of long-haul travelers who routinely cross multiple time zones. Further research is expected to explore whether targeted probiotic strains can accelerate gut microbiome recovery after intercontinental flights. For now, the takeaway is clear: preparing the body for a long flight deserves as much attention as booking the seat.
